Here are our documents.

=== Notes ===
Sample (fictional)

Quillmere Rolling Library
Board meeting notes, October 21, 2026, Vashti Bend Community Room

Present: June Okafor-Reyes (board chair), Abner Whitlock (treasurer), Marisol Quennell (executive director), Pete Danforth (driver-librarian), Lila Ferrand (board member)

Item 3: Beaumont-Tully Rural Literacy Fund

Marisol reported that program officer Celeste Harrow at the Beaumont-Tully Rural Literacy Fund invited us to present Route Eighteen at their December 4 review. We will ask for $85,000 toward the $148,000 total. The county capital award of $40,000 is committed, and the spring donor campaign covers the last $23,000.

June asked for a short slide deck to go with the presentation. Marisol will own it. Draft to the board by November 20, 2026, final to Celeste by November 27.

Instructions the board agreed on for the deck:

1. Keep it to eight slides or fewer. Ms. Harrow said reviewers get ten minutes per applicant.
2. Open with the problem: 11 missed stops last year, all from the 2009 vehicle, and four north-county schools with 310 students waiting to join.

response.draft:
Slide 1: Route Eighteen: 11 Missed Stops, 310 Students Waiting
Quillmere Rolling Library, presented to the Beaumont-Tully Rural Literacy Fund, December 4, 2026
Last year we missed 11 of 292 scheduled stops, and our 2009 bookmobile caused every one
The bookmobile passed 214,000 miles this spring
Four north-county schools have asked to join: Dunmore, Pike Hollow, Sayer Flat and East Kettle
Together they enroll 310 K-6 students, and none of them has a school librarian
With one aging vehicle we cannot add them

Slide 2: What We Do Today (FY2026)
We serve 14 rural elementary schools with no school librarian, each more than 25 miles from a public library
We reach 1,180 K-6 students, with a visit every other week for 36 weeks plus 40 summer stops
We made 281 of 292 stops (96 percent)
Students checked out 21,460 items, up from 18,930 in FY2025, with a 91 percent return rate
We issued 846 new county library cards to students
52 of 61 teachers used our new classroom crate loans, which account for about 4,100 checkouts
Our finances are stable: $191,250 in revenue against $186,400 in expenses, and the county contract and Voss Foundation grant are renewed for FY2027

Slide 3: One Vehicle Near the End of Its Life
October: a transmission line failed
February: the bookmobile failed its brake inspection
June: it overheated twice
Vehicle costs rose from $19,700 to $31,900 in one year, almost all of it repairs
Each missed stop means a class waits four weeks between visits, not two
"Bookmobile Tuesday is the only day the whole class runs to the window. When you missed in February, three kids asked me if you were coming back." – Dorrie Akin, third-grade teacher, Fallow Creek Elementary

Slide 4: The Plan: Route Eighteen
We will buy a used high-roof cargo van, refitted with shelving and a wheelchair lift
The van will run a new north route to the four waiting schools
The 2009 bookmobile will stay on the shorter southern route through FY2028 while we save for its replacement
With two vehicles, a breakdown on one route no longer cancels every stop
At full service: 18 schools, about 1,490 students, 324 school stops a year

Slide 5: Route Eighteen Budget: $148,000
Used high-roof cargo van: $74,000
Refit (shelving, wheelchair lift, inverter, mobile hotspot): $18,500
Opening collection for four new schools (2,400 books): $21,600
Added driver-librarian hours, 0.5 FTE, year one: $26,400
Driver training, vehicle signage, launch visits: $3,500
Contingency: $4,000
Total: $148,000 (one-time costs plus first-year added operating cost)

Slide 6: How We Will Pay for It
Corrow County Library District one-time capital award: $40,000 (committed)
Beaumont-Tully Rural Literacy Fund: $85,000 (this request)
Spring 2027 donor campaign: $23,000 (planned)
Total: $148,000
Your $85,000 covers part of the project, not all of it

Slide 7: Reading Results, With Their Limits
At the 6 schools that shared data (188 students), the share of third graders reading at or above grade level went from 41 percent in spring 2025 to 49 percent in spring 2026
Six schools is not all 14, and the schools that agreed to share may be the most engaged ones
We had no comparison group
State-funded reading tutors worked in four of those six schools in the same year
We cannot separate our effect from the tutors' effect, and we do not claim this gain as ours
What we can say: the schools that borrowed the most books from us were also the schools where scores went up
Next year: we will collect benchmark data from all 14 schools and track checkouts per student

Slide 8: Timeline, Goals and Our Request
March 2027: Route Eighteen fully funded
Spring 2027: buy and refit the van
June 2027: summer stops begin on the north route
August 2027: full school service begins at 18 schools
FY2027 goals: miss no more than 3 stops, collect benchmark data from all 14 current schools, have the van running north-county summer stops by June 2027
Our request: $85,000 from the Beaumont-Tully Rural Literacy Fund
Marisol Quennell, Executive Director, Quillmere Rolling Library, Vashti Bend
